The European layer then tidied the categories without changing the shape underneath, which is why a student who learns one of the four can read the others quickly.

claim: Stem: 'Austria's vineyard classification is being written privately before it is written into law'; exp: 'The state's own contribution is the Riedenwein tier, which protects the site name but ranks nothing ... the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard.'

It reserves both terms for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, with lower maximum yields and hand harvest. Regional wine committees propose the classifications, and a site can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after Erste Lage. First statutory classifications were expected from the 2025 vintage. The ÖTW model was written into law, so the law now does rank sites and the claim that it ranks nothing is out of date.

finalFix: Stem: "Austria's vineyard classifications were written privately before the law made room for one. Which association classifies Erste Lage sites in the Danube regions, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?" Keep the accepted answers (ÖTW, STK). The Pinot Noir was the Martin Ray clone. What made Hanzell Burgundian was the winemaking: Brad Webb's small French oak barrels, induced malolactic and temperature-controlled stainless steel. The clones were not Burgundian.

claim: The explanation says the sugar in a botrytis wine is a jam-sense preservative that denies microbes the water they need in the open bottle.

Jam and honey are 60 to 80 percent sugar, and it takes that much to push water activity below the thresholds that stop microbes (Wikipedia, Water activity: honey aw 0.5 to 0.7, most moulds stopped at 0.80). At the concentrations found in sweet wine, residual sugar feeds spoilage yeasts rather than starving them. Z. bailii grows faster at 10% glucose than at 1% and is most resistant to preservatives at 10 to 20% sugar, and wine is on its list of spoiled products. This is why sweet wines are prone to refermentation and are allowed, and routinely given, much more SO2 than dry wines. Wikipedia's Sulfite article: sweeter wines contain more sulfites than drier ones. An opened sweet wine lasts because the sugar masks early oxidation, helped by acidity, alcohol and its high sulphur dioxide. Osmotic starvation of microbes plays no part. The keyed answer (sugar) can stay.

A survey of Brazilian reds found that 4-EP:4-EG ran from 1.37 to 21.98. It was higher in Cabernet Sauvignon, and the paper cites published ratios of 10:1 for Cabernet Sauvignon and 8:1 for Merlot. Laboratories such as ETS report both compounds separately for exactly this reason. The rest of the question and the key (4-ethylphenol) are correct.

It measured ratios in Brazilian reds running from 1.37 to 21.98, and it says that matches the 1.6 to 38 range reported by Pollnitz et al. (2000) and Henschke et al. (2004). It also found a statistically significant difference between Cabernet Sauvignon (9.24) and Merlot (7.51). It cites 10:1 for Cabernet and 8:1 for Merlot (Pollnitz), 8:1 for Bordeaux (Chatonnet 1992) and about 9:1 for Chilean wines.
